_purpose: Research log. Key = the specific thing looked up; value = what was found, verdict, and the exact URLs so it is never researched twice.
_rules: One entry per distinct question. Update the entry when re-checking a version. Never delete a URL that a decision rests on.

schema.question: what was being decided
findings: facts, with version/tag attached
schema.verdict: what we do because of it

entries.question: What Python and libraries exist in the build sandbox, and can pip install?
findings: Python 3.11.2, pip 23.0.1, 2 vCPU, 3.6 GiB RAM, no swap, ~20 GB disk.
Nothing preinstalled: no numpy, zstandard, torch, lightning, transformers, pytest, maturin.
pip download from PyPI works (numpy 2.4.6 wheel fetched at ~100 MB/s).
zstandard 0.25.0 has manylinux/mac/windows cp311 wheels; torch 2.15.0 wheels: 514 MiB linux x86_64, 461 MiB aarch64, 132 MiB macOS arm64, 121 MiB win_amd64.
torch wheels exist for cp311-cp314 plus free-threaded cp314t.
entries.verdict: Pure-Python archx is buildable and testable here; torch integration tests are local-possible but heavy (514 MiB download) so full matrices go to CI.

entries.question: Which hosts can this sandbox reach?
findings: Reachable: github.com, api.github.com, codeload.github.com, pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org, registry.npmjs.org.

Blocked (curl 000, no connection): static.rust-lang.org, sh.rustup.rs, crates.io, index.crates.io, static.crates.io, docs.rs, doc.rust-lang.org, raw.githubusercontent.com, objects.githubusercontent.com, release-assets.githubusercontent.com, docs.github.com, example.com.
github.com release-asset URLs answer 302 but the redirect target is blocked.
entries.verdict: No Rust toolchain can be installed here, ever. GitHub file content must be read through the API (contents endpoint), not raw. Docs must be written from API-read sources.

entries.question: What can the GitHub token do in this repo?
findings: actions/workflows: 200 (currently 0 workflows). actions/runs: 200. actions/artifacts: 200.
actions/secrets: 403. actions/variables: 403. actions/permissions: 403. branches/main/protection: 403.
contents: 200 read. X-Oauth-Scopes header empty; fine-grained token style permissions.
entries.verdict: We can create commits and read workflow metadata, but never logs, artifacts, secrets or variables. Therefore every workflow must commit its results into the repo, which is exactly the user's stated workaround.

entries.question: Which public optimizer hook does archx attach to, and since which version?
findings: v2.0.0 has register_step_pre_hook / register_step_post_hook (lines ~298/320).
v1.13.1 has only the internal profile_hook_step decorator, no public hook.
post hooks run after func(*args, **kwargs) inside profile_hook_step, i.e. after the weights are updated.
profile_hook_step patches the optimizer CLASS lazily on first step (_patch_step_function), so the first step pays a one-time patch cost.
entries.verdict: attach() uses optimizer.register_step_post_hook; minimum torch is 2.0 for attach(), 2.1 for the accumulate-grad hook. Deltas therefore come from a shadow copy of the previous step (Architecture section 4).

entries.question: Since which torch version can we observe gradients cheaply without a backward hook?
findings: Tensor.register_post_accumulate_grad_hook exists at v2.1.0 and v2.9.0, absent at v2.0.0.
It is defined on torch._tensor.Tensor (line ~572 at v2.4.0), not on nn.Module.
The hook fires right after the gradient for that tensor has accumulated, before zero_grad.
entries.verdict: Preferred gradient-norm path on torch >= 2.1: one hook per tracked parameter, no full backward hook. Fallback: read param.grad in the optimizer pre-step hook.

entries.question: What does the HF Trainer callback expose, and when can archx read gradients and the trainer object?
findings: Callback methods take (args, state, control, **kwargs); the Trainer is reachable via kwargs when provided.
Available: on_train_begin/end, on_epoch_begin/end, on_step_begin/end, on_pre_optimizer_step, on_optimizer_step, on_substep_end, on_log, on_evaluate, on_save, on_predict.
on_pre_optimizer_step and on_optimizer_step are absent in 4.44 and present in 4.46.
Inner loop order in current trainer.py: optimizer.step() -> model.zero_grad() -> global_step += 1 -> on_step_end, so gradients are zero by on_step_end.
entries.verdict: Default gradient capture is an optimizer post-hook on trainer.optimizer (version independent). on_pre_optimizer_step is used when >= 4.46. Minimum supported transformers for Tier 2 is 4.46, with a silent fallback below it.

entries.question: What is wrapped by Accelerate/DDP and how does that affect parameter access?
findings: Trainer creates an Accelerator; model may become DistributedDataParallel (extra 'module.' name prefix) and the optimizer becomes AcceleratedOptimizer (its step() is what runs, and it can skip steps).
In the DDP case every rank holds identical full parameters; in FSDP/ZeRO cases it does not.
entries.verdict: Names come from accelerator.unwrap_model(model); the observed optimizer is the wrapped one; only the main process writes to the file. Sharded setups are detected and degraded (Architecture 5.4).

entries.question: Do TRL SFTTrainer/DPOTrainer and Axolotl's trainer accept a plain TrainerCallback?
findings: class SFTTrainer(_BaseTrainer) and class DPOTrainer(_BaseTrainer) in current TRL.
class AxolotlTrainer(...) in axolotl core/trainers/base.py subclasses the same Trainer hierarchy.
DPO-style trainers run more than one backward per optimizer step (policy and reference).
entries.verdict: No separate adapters: one ArchxCallback covers all three. Step accounting must key on optimizer steps, not backward passes.

entries.question: Which Lightning callbacks exist, and where are gradients available?
findings: Hooks include on_fit_start/end, on_train_batch_start/end, on_before_backward, on_after_backward, on_before_optimizer_step, on_before_zero_grad, on_validation_*, on_save_checkpoint, on_exception.
Automatic optimization runs the optimizer with a closure (Closure/_optimizer_step), and may call zero_grad inside the closure; manual optimization does not.
Lightning can call optimizer.step() itself or via the closure, so one step per batch cannot be assumed.
entries.verdict: Use on_before_optimizer_step (post-clipping gradients) as the default capture point, plus an optimizer post-hook for deltas; count steps from loop state. on_after_backward is available for pre-clipping norms.

entries.question: Which zstd binding should a pure-Python archx use?
findings: zstandard 0.25.0 windows/mac/linux wheels for cp311 and friends, ~5 MiB.
CPython 3.14 ships a stdlib compression.zstd package (Lib/compression/zstd present on the 3.14 branch).
lz4 exists but trades ratio for speed; not needed for a background writer.
entries.verdict: Use zstandard, with a stdlib compression.zstd path on Python >= 3.14 and a pure-fallback 'no compression' mode when neither is importable.

entries.question: Can a Rust core (Rust + PyO3/maturin) be built in this environment?
findings: No rustc/cargo/rustup installed; apt has no rustc candidate.
Every Rust distribution and crate host is unreachable from the sandbox.
Only GitHub, PyPI and npm are reachable.
entries.verdict: A Rust core can never be compiled or unit-tested locally. The v1 core is Python; a native accelerator is an optional later add-on built only on CI. Recorded as a decision for the user in Open_Questions Q4.

entries.question: Does the trigger-file workflow work, can all three runners commit results back, and what hardware do they give us?
findings: Push touching Actions/triggers/tests.txt started workflow 'tests' automatically (run 43052619656).
3 of 3 matrix jobs succeeded: ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest.
Each runner committed its own file (three separate bot commits, no conflicts) - the rebase-retry script works.
Measured cpu_count=4 on Linux x86_64, Windows X64; macOS-26.7.2 arm64. Python 3.11.18 / 3.11.9.
gathered local pulls worked as the only way to read results (Actions logs remain unreadable).
entries.verdict: The CI spine is proven and is the transport for everything heavy. 4 vCPU per runner is 2x the sandbox, which confirms the 'heavy work goes to Actions' rule.

entries.question: Which package names are free for this project on PyPI and npm?
findings: PyPI archx: 200, version 0.1.1, 'A framework to explore the design space of computer systems' - unrelated project.
PyPI archx-mdl, archxmdl, archx_mdl, archnemix, archx-lifeline: 404 (free).
npm archx: 404 (free). npm archx-mdl: 404 (free).
npm username existence cannot be checked unauthenticated (401 for both archx and archnemix).
PEP 503 normalises archx.mdl and archx-mdl to the same project name, so both pip spellings resolve.
entries.verdict: Distribution archx.mdl on PyPI, npm archx as a signpost, import/CLI stay archx. Re-check right before publishing; availability can change.

entries.question: What did implementing the container teach that the spec did not say?
findings: struct.Struct with '<' uses standard sizes and no alignment: '<HBBQIIII' is exactly 28 bytes, not 32.
argparse's --version action raises SystemExit(0) instead of returning, so callers/tests must expect it.
A footer shares the byte space a block prefix would occupy, so readers must test the END magic before any size-based branch.
The step must live in the block prefix (8 bytes) for recovery to rebuild an index without decompressing payloads.
pytest -q prints only dots when everything passes; the counts have to be derived from the dot line, not from a summary sentence.
entries.verdict: Block prefix is 28 bytes with the step inside; reader checks END magic first; test records parse dots into counts.

entries.question: Which delta encoder is smallest, and at what error, on realistic training deltas?
findings: 256x256 f32, 1% moved: sparse 3,404 B exact (77x); int8 2,098 B at 8.9e-3 (125x); lowrank refused.
256x256 f32, all moved: int8 56,190 B at 1.1e-2 (4.7x); sparse refused; lowrank refused; dense_raw 242,475 B exact (1.1x).
rank-4 structure: lowrank found rank 4 exactly, 7,680 B (34.1x, 8.4e-8); int8 52,266 B at 1.5e-2; dense_raw 243,459 B exact (1.1x).
Sparse vs int8 crossover: int8 is smaller at every density from 0.1% to 100% when error is allowed; sparse only wins when exactness is required.
Byte-plane shuffle: sparse 1% 4,533 -> 7,774 B (0.58x, a loss); dense 242,473 -> 227,533 (1.07x); rank-4 243,457 -> 233,010 (1.04x). An all-zero tensor is shuffle-invariant.
Low-rank refuses random noise at rank 8 with a 1e-3 budget (relative error stays ~0.9).
Re-run 2026-11-12 after the Phase 3 source changes: identical encoder choices, and the dense_raw figures moved by <3% (zstd stream layout), which is the noise floor of these scripts.

Claim 5 re-run on the same date, 262,144 params, 200 steps: none 3.63 ms; adaptive default 3.75 ms (+3.4%, 18,443 KiB, 23 stored / 177 skipped); every step 4.53 ms (+24.7%, 57,671 KiB). The run varies by a percent between invocations, so read these as a range, not a precise figure.
entries.verdict: Policy is per tensor: exact path = sparse or dense_raw, lossy path = int8 unless the delta is genuinely low rank. Shuffle stays off by default. Any ratio quoted in the docs must come from these scripts.

entries.question: What does attaching the recorder actually cost per optimizer step, and which half costs it?
sources: local timings, 2 vCPU sandbox, torch 2.15.0+cu132 on CPU
findings: Charged cost of the recorder's own code: 0.119 ms per step with data_level=none, 0.140 ms with segments, on a 19.2 ms step (512-wide MLP, batch 1024, median of 25).
Wall-clock overhead of timing two whole runs is unusable here: the same loop varies by +/-8% between runs, and the first measurement of the same code gave +550%, +320% and -0.6% on consecutive runs.
Taking the snapshot twice per anchor cost +17% before it was removed; hashing and compressing the batch on the training thread cost +81% before it was moved to the writer thread.
content_id (blake2b-16) of 128 KiB = 210 us, of 2 MiB = 3.4 ms; zstd level 3 of 128 KiB = ~530 us; detach().cpu().numpy().tobytes() of a 2 MiB tensor = 150 us.
Global grad norm via pow(2).sum().item() per tensor = 40 us; via one numpy dot per tensor = 19 us, on a 6-tensor model.
On a 0.3 ms toy step the same code is a 350-650% overhead because framework dispatch dominates; a fixed percentage budget is only meaningful on a step big enough to have a cost.
entries.verdict: Measure by charging our own code, not by differencing two noisy runs. Data hashing and compression belong on the writer thread; the one unavoidable training-thread cost is one buffer copy, and data_level is the escape hatch. The <5% claim is stated for the weight half, where it is 0.6%.

entries.question: If the training process is killed while recording, what survives, and what must the recorder do to keep the join?
sources: Tests/integration/test_crash_recovery.py (child process, real SIGKILL on POSIX, terminate on Windows)
findings: A killed process never writes a footer, so the file is 'crashed' by definition; Reader(allow_torn=True) already read a valid prefix before any recovery, and recover_in_place then makes it closed and re-indexed without inventing blocks.
Data written only at close was lost entirely on a kill: the deltas survived and every batch did not. The product's answer became 'the weights moved' with no cause.
Writing data after each stored step introduced two ordering rules: a shard before the segment pointing at it, and movement before the data explaining it.
A segment may still not name a step the file has not reached; the flush that writes a segment is clamped to the previous step, because the EVENT for the current step is appended after the flush.
A writer-thread exception used to kill the thread silently while training continued: a dict-mutation race at step 22 lost 4000 further steps with no signal.
A segment stated several times (as it grows) is resolved by last-statement-wins in Timeline.segments(); the raw block list is append-only and not the reader's view.
entries.verdict: Write data during the run, in a fixed order, under a lock; state a segment only for steps already on disk; never let the writer thread die without recording the fault in an INFO block and re-raising it from close().

entries.question: How can torch be installed so the adapter is tested for real instead of skipped?
sources: https://pypi.org/pypi/torch/json (2.15.0, CUDA build as the default wheel)
findings: pip install torch installs 2.15.0+cu132; import fails with ValueError: libcublasLt.so.*[0-9] not found.
pip install --no-deps torch installs but stays unimportable.
The CPU index https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu is unreachable from this sandbox: TLS handshake closed (SSLZeroReturnError), no version list returned.

Installing nvidia-cublas, -cuda-runtime, -cuda-nvrtc, -cudnn-cu13, -cufft, -cusolver, -cusparse, -curand, -nvjitlink, -nccl-cu13, -nvtx, -cuda-cupti, -cusparselt-cu13, -cufile and -nvshmem-cu13 makes import work; nvshmem is the one pip does not pull in itself (libnvshmem_host.so.3).
pip then reports version conflicts against torch's pins (nccl, cusparselt, setuptools); the CPU path still imports and runs every step, so the warnings are cosmetic here.
Cost: 8 GB of disk out of 20 GB free, about 2.5 minutes of download.
entries.verdict: Install the nvidia dependency set to test the adapter locally; keep pytest.importorskip('torch') in the test module so a runner without torch skips with a reason instead of failing. Documented in Docs/Workaround.md.

entries.question: Where do loss, gradient norm, learning rate and user annotations belong in the container?
findings: The spec already allocated EVENT (5) for 'timeline entry: step, kind, values (loss, lr, grad norms, timings)' and ANNOT (7) for 'user annotation: step, event name, detail'.
The first implementation wrote both into EVENT, so a reader could not separate what the run measured from what the user declared.
META claimed capability_tier 1 unconditionally while no tier-1 value was ever written.
A tier is only meaningful compared with its own data: tier 2 without tier 1 is a claim the file contradicts.
entries.verdict: EVENT carries observations only, ANNOT carries annotations only, and the achieved tier plus every missing field with a reason goes into an INFO capability block written at close, after the data that proves tier 2.
